basics.name: William Zhou
basics.label: Student
basics.summary: Electrical and Computer engineering student broadly interested in autonomous systems and perception

work.name: Biomechatronics Lab, North Carolina State University
highlights: Designed and fabricated hardware in Fusion 360 for a novel prosthetic hand with tactile feedback and robotic arm transport system.
Developed user‑control interfaces in C++ using Arduino ESP32 microcontrollers and PlatformIO, enabling intuitive manipulation of the robotic arm.
Authored an abstract and poster on prosthetic robotic arm technology that was accepted for presentation at the IEEE International Conference on Advanced Intelligent Mechatronics (AIM) 2024.

work.name: Triangle Aerial Drone Association
highlights: Dedicated to promoting drone technology in the North Carolina Research Triangle region.
Mentored and taught two drone robotics teams that achieved top‑3 national placements at the National REC Aerial Drone Competition.
Developed a comprehensive technical resource guide analyzing competition drone source code, reverse‑engineering autonomy stacks, and implementing optimal navigation methods.

work.name: College of Engineering, North Carolina State University
highlights: Brainstormed, filmed, and edited videos for the College of Engineering’s social‑media channels.
Collaborated with faculty, students, and other departments to produce promotional content showcasing engineering programs and research initiatives.
Utilized Adobe Premiere Pro to deliver high‑quality video content on tight turnaround schedules.

work.name: Acoustofludic Lab, Duke University
highlights: Advanced an innovative acoustic‑radiation‑force based technique for precise drug delivery into microfluidic droplets.
Optimized fluid circuit design using AutoCAD to determine the ideal convergence angle, enhancing droplet‑formation efficiency for acoustofluidic beam applications.
Designed and refined figures for poster presentations, documented iteration changes, and contributed to testing microfluidic devices with oscilloscopes and high‑speed microscopy.
